scenarios.name: Bundle, no board, then a follow-up

card.problem: Explain what a Bundle is in Android and when to use it
card.heard: explain Bundle and when to use it
card.say: A Bundle is a simple container that holds key-value pairs. Android uses it to pass small data between screens and to save state. For example, I put an ID in a Bundle when I open a detail screen. I also use it in onSaveInstanceState, so the screen can rebuild after process death. I keep it small, because it gets serialized.

results.detail: none
PASS: The SAY line plainly defines a Bundle as a key-value container and explains its uses without any code.

card.problem: Explain what a Bundle is in Android and when to use it
card.constraints: ["Bundle must stay small because of the Binder limit"]
card.heard: what happens if the Bundle gets too large
card.say: It fails. A Bundle goes through Binder, and Binder has a hard limit of about 1 MB for the whole transaction. If the Bundle is too big, the system throws a TransactionTooLargeException. The screen may crash, or the data just doesn't arrive. So I never put large data in a Bundle.

results.detail: none
PASS: The SAY explains the Binder ~1 MB limit and TransactionTooLargeException, directly answering what happens when a Bundle is too large rather than restating the definition.

transcript: Interviewer: Can you explain what a Bundle is in Android and when you would use it?
Interviewer: What happens if the Bundle gets too large?

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-like chat screen on Android: user sends a message, AI reply streams in, list scrolls, user can send again during a reply

card.say: Before I design, let me check the scope. The user types a message and sees the AI reply stream in, token by token. The list scrolls, and the user can send again while a reply is still coming. I'd keep history and offline storage out of the first version. Does that match what you want?

results.detail: none

PASS: SAY opens by scoping the design (streaming replies, scrolling, sending during a reply, deferring history/offline) and asks for confirmation, which is a step-by-step design start rather than a full essay or code.

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-like chat screen on Android: user sends a message, AI reply streams in, list scrolls, user can send again during a reply
card.heard: write the ViewModel that holds the message list
card.say: Okay, I'll write the ViewModel now. It holds the message list in a StateFlow, so the screen redraws when a message changes. Each message has an id, a role and the text so far. When the AI reply streams in, I update the last message in place instead of adding a new one each time.
card.type: add@ChatViewModel: data class Message( ⏎     val id: String, ⏎     val role: Role, ⏎     val text: String, ⏎     val isStreaming: Boolean = false ⏎ ) ⏎  ⏎ enum class Role { USER, ASSISTANT } ⏎  ⏎ class ChatViewModel : ViewModel() { ⏎     private val _messages = MutableStateFlow<List<Message>>(emptyList()) ⏎     val messages: StateFlow<List<Message>> = _messages.asStateFlow() ⏎  ⏎     fun send(text: String) { ⏎         val userMsg = Message(id = UUID.randomUUID().toString(), role = Role.USER, text = text) ⏎         val replyId = UUID.randomUUID().toString() ⏎         val reply = Message(id = replyId, role = Role.ASSISTANT, text = "", isStreaming = true) ⏎         _messages.update { it + userMsg + reply } ⏎     } ⏎  ⏎     fun onToken(replyId: String, token: String) { ⏎         _messages.update { list -> ⏎             list.map { msg -> ⏎                 if (msg.id == replyId) msg.copy(text = msg.text + token) else msg ⏎             } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎  ⏎     fun onDone(replyId: String) { ⏎         _messages.update { list -> ⏎             list.map { msg -> ⏎                 if (msg.id == replyId) msg.copy(isStreaming = false) else msg ⏎             } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }

results.detail: add@ChatViewModel: data class Message( ⏎     val id: String, ⏎     val role: Role, ⏎     val text: String, ⏎     val isS

PASS: The SAY section provides a brief spoken lead-in explaining the StateFlow approach and streaming updates, and the TYPE section contains a compact Kotlin ViewModel with a Message data class, Role enum, and ChatViewModel handling the message list.

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-like chat screen on Android: user sends a message, AI reply streams in, list scrolls, user can send again during a reply
card.heard: why StateFlow over LiveData
card.say: There are two reasons. First, StateFlow is a plain Kotlin flow, so I can combine it with the streaming tokens and test it without Android. Second, it always has a current value, so a new screen gets the last list right away. LiveData is tied to the lifecycle and is harder to use outside the UI. Do you want me to switch to LiveData, or keep StateFlow?

results.detail: PASS: The SAY explains StateFlow's advantages (plain Kotlin flow, testable without Android, always has current value) and contrasts with LiveData's lifecycle coupling, directly answering the question about the chat screen's message list.

transcript: Interviewer: How would you design a chat screen like ChatGPT on Android?
Interviewer: Okay, can you write the ViewModel that holds the message list?
Interviewer: Why did you pick StateFlow over LiveData there?

scenarios.name: Switch A to B while the board still shows A

card.problem: Implement load() in the ViewModel using RxJava
card.adopted: Switch load() to Kotlin Flow with StateFlow
card.heard: switch from RxJava to Kotlin Flow
card.say: Okay, I'll switch this part to Flow. I'll collect the flow in viewModelScope, so it stops when the ViewModel is cleared. I'll keep the result in a StateFlow, so the screen can observe it and get the latest value.
card.type: replace@ChatViewModel: class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepository) : ViewModel() { ⏎     private val _messages = MutableStateFlow<List<Message>>(emptyList()) ⏎     val messages: StateFlow<List<Message>> = _messages ⏎  ⏎     fun load() { ⏎         viewModelScope.launch { ⏎             repo.messages() ⏎                 .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) ⏎                 .collect { _messages.value = it } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }

results.detail: Switch load() to Kotlin Flow with StateFlow
PASS: SAY frames the switch as a plan ("I'll switch..."), doesn't claim completion, and the TYPE migrates load() to Flow with viewModelScope and StateFlow, dropping RxJava.

card.problem: Walk through the chat API contract and how the Android client consumes it
card.heard: Walk me through this API
card.say: This is a feed endpoint, not the chat stream. The app calls it with a cursor and a limit, and gets back a page of posts. Each post has an id, a time, the content and the author. The pagination metadata tells the client where the next page starts and whether it has reached the end. So the client keeps the cursor, asks for the next page, and stops when reachedEnd is true.
card.then: I'd explain how the client stores the cursor and handles a page that comes back empty.

scenarios.name: Follow-up inside a follow-up, then back

card.problem: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed
card.heard: Who owns the cache, the repository or the data source?
card.say: The data source owns the cache. The repository just decides when to use it. The local data source holds the database and the in-memory copy. The remote data source holds the network calls. The repository reads from the local one first, then asks the remote one to refresh.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY explicitly states the data source owns the cache and clarifies the repository only decides when to use it.

card.problem: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed
card.heard: Okay, makes sense. Please continue with the data layer.
card.say: Okay, I'll continue. Next I'll add the local data source, which owns the Room database and the DAO. The repository will call it to read the cached articles and to save fresh ones.
card.type: add@LocalDataSource: class LocalDataSource(private val dao: ArticleDao) { ⏎     fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> = dao.observeAll() ⏎     suspend fun save(articles: List<Article>) = dao.upsertAll(articles) ⏎ }
card.then: Then I'll add the remote data source for the network call, and wire both into the repository.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY line resumes the data layer design by introducing the local data source and its role, without re-explaining the repository's purpose.

transcript: Interviewer: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed.
Interviewer: Wait, why a repository at all?
Interviewer: And who owns the cache, the repository or the data source?

scenarios.name: Switch problems and return

card.problem: Let's pause that. New question: what is the difference between a Service and a WorkManager job?
card.heard: Service vs WorkManager
card.say: A Service is a general Android component that runs in the background. It keeps running until something stops it, and I manage its lifetime myself. WorkManager is for work that must finish, even if the app closes or the phone restarts. It retries and respects limits like battery and network. So for a one-off background task, I'd use a Service.

results.detail: FAIL: The SAY section ends with incorrect guidance ("for a one-off background task, I'd use a Service")—one-off guaranteed work is precisely WorkManager's use case, so the answer is misleading despite covering the basic distinction.

card.problem: Design an image loading library for Android: load an image URL into an ImageView with memory and disk cache, off the main thread
card.heard: back to the image loading library
card.say: Okay, back to the image loading library. The goal is to load an image URL into an ImageView, with a memory cache and a disk cache, and all the heavy work off the main thread. I'd start with the request flow: the caller gives a URL and an ImageView, and the library checks the memory cache first. If it's a miss, it checks the disk cache, and only then goes to the network. Each step runs on a background dispatcher, and the result comes back to the main thread to set the image.
card.then: I'd go into the memory cache design next, or the threading, whichever you prefer.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY line resumes the image loading library design by restating the goal and outlining the request flow, memory/disk cache checks, and background threading.

transcript: Interviewer: Design an image loading library for Android.
Interviewer: Let's pause that. New question: what is the difference between a Service and a WorkManager job?
Interviewer: Good. Now let's go back to the image loading library.

scenarios.name: An early constraint survives a long discussion

card.problem: Design a notes app that works fully offline (hard requirement)
card.heard: What would you build next?
card.say: Next I'd build the sync layer, but it stays optional. The app must work fully offline, so local Room is the source of truth. A WorkManager job would push local changes to the server when a network is there. Each note gets a local ID and a "dirty" flag, so a failed upload just retries later. The UI never waits for the network.

results.detail: ["Must work fully offline, hard requirement"]
PASS: The card proposes a sync layer that is explicitly optional, keeps local Room as the source of truth, and ensures the UI never waits on the network—fully respecting the hard offline requirement.
